newsitem.title: INDONESIA: U.S. not concerned about Southeast Asian arms race.
newsitem.headline: U.S. not concerned about Southeast Asian arms race.

text.p: U.S. arms control envoy Thomas Graham said on Thursday that Washington had no concerns about an arms buildup in Southeast Asia despite recent purchases of modern weaponry by a number of countries.
"In general, we think that the situation is good here," Graham, special representative of the president for arms control, non-proliferation and disarmament, told a news conference.
"As we see it right now, we do not think that the expenditures on arms in this region are out of line and we don't see an arms race here on the horizon," Graham said.
He said all seven members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) supported the various treaties on non-proliferation as well as those on chemical and biological weapons.
"Compared to some regions of the world, ASEAN is a relatively stable place," he said.

Analysts have pointed to the purchase of increasingly sophisticated jet fighters by Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia in recent years as well as the expansion of the Thai and Indonesian navies as evidence of a regional arms race.
But governments concerned have said they are replacing weapons rather than matching purchases by neighbouring countries.

Graham said the United States was committed to signing the Southeast Asian Nuclear Weapons Free Zone treaty if the signatories made changes so it applied only to the land areas of the respective nations rather than the oceans surrounding them.

"The nuclear weapons free zone, established by the Treaty of Bangkok, should be limited to the territories of the parties and not expanded out into the high seas where...it inevitably comes into conflict with the Law of the Sea Convention," he said.
ASEAN comprises Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
